dialect: Standard Swahili (Kiswahili sanifu), as taught in Tanzania and Kenya

profile.noun_citation: singular with class prefix (plural noted in discussion when useful)
profile.pronunciation_convention: IPA (broad); spoken = stress hint on the penultimate syllable
profile.grammar_notes: Identity: ni (negative si), a zero-copula-like particle invariant for person. Location and state: -ko/-po/-mo with subject prefixes (niko, uko, yuko...). Existence: kuna/pana/mna (hakuna). Possession: kuwa na (nina, una, ana...; negative sina, huna, hana). People: subject prefixes ni-/u-/a-/tu-/m-/wa- are a closed set; independent pronouns mimi, wewe, yeye, sisi, ninyi/nyinyi, wao are a closed set. Tense/aspect: infixes -na- (present), -li- (past), -ta- (future), -me- (perfect); negation changes the prefix (si-, hu-, ha-, hatu-, ham-, hawa-) and past negative uses -ku-. Questions: intonation, or je at the start; question words nini, nani, wapi, lini, gani, vipi, -ngapi. Want/can/must: -taka, -weza, lazima/-bidi. Go/come: -enda, -ja (monosyllabic verbs keep ku- in some tenses: ninakuja, nilikuja). Noun classes come in singular/plural pairs (m-/wa-, m-/mi-, ji-/ma-, ki-/vi-, n-/n-, u-, ku-) that drive agreement on adjectives, possessives (-angu, -ako) and verbs; the class system is a closed set too big for a 12-term list. Politeness is lexical (tafadhali, shikamoo/marahaba, samahani), not grammatical. No articles; no grammatical gender.
